summary: Vorasidenib (Voranigo) is an oral dual inhibitor of mutant IDH1 and IDH2 approved in 2024 for adults and adolescents 12 years and older with Grade 2 astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma harboring a susceptible IDH1 or IDH2 mutation following surgery, based on the INDIGO Phase 3 trial. By blocking mutant IDH enzymes it lowers the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate and slows tumor growth. The adult dose is 40 mg once daily (pediatric weight-based: 40 mg if 40 kg or more, 20 mg if under 40 kg) with or without food until progression or unacceptable toxicity. There is no boxed warning; key risks are hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations that can progress to hepatic failure, necrosis, or autoimmune hepatitis, and embryo-fetal toxicity requiring nonhormonal contraception during and for 3 months after treatment.

moa: Vorasidenib inhibits mutant forms of isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IDH1/IDH2). Mutant IDH enzymes convert alpha-ketoglutarate to the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), which impairs cellular differentiation and promotes glioma growth. By blocking mutant IDH1 and IDH2, vorasidenib lowers 2-HG levels, helping restore differentiation and slowing growth of susceptible-mutant Grade 2 astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma. It crosses the blood-brain barrier to act within the central nervous system.

absolute: Known serious hypersensitivity to vorasidenib or any excipient
relative: Pre-existing significant hepatic impairment (limited data; hepatotoxicity risk)
monitor: Hormonal contraceptives (may be less reliable; use nonhormonal methods)
Other seizure-threshold-lowering drugs in glioma patients

preg: Based on animal findings, vorasidenib can cause fetal harm including resorptions, decreased fetal weight, and delayed ossification. Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective nonhormonal contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose, since vorasidenib may render hormonal contraceptives ineffective.
lact: There are no data on the presence of vorasidenib in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment.
renal: No dose adjustment is established for renal impairment. Data in severe renal impairment are limited; monitor closely if used.
hepatic: No established dose adjustment is defined by hepatic function. Vorasidenib can cause transaminase elevations leading to hepatic failure, necrosis, or autoimmune hepatitis. Monitor liver function every 2 weeks during the first 2 months, then monthly for the first 2 years and as indicated; withhold, reduce, or discontinue based on severity per labeling.

missed: If a dose is missed by less than 6 hours, take the missed dose right away. If 6 or more hours have passed, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the usual time. If vomiting occurs after a dose, do not take an extra dose; resume at the usual time.
overdose: There is no specific antidote for vorasidenib overdose. Exaggerated hepatotoxicity and constitutional effects may occur. Withhold treatment, monitor liver function tests closely, and provide supportive care. Contact Poison Help (1-800-222-1222).
